On Nov 30, 2015, at 11:53 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I’d also love to talk about CVODE, the refactor, etc.  We might

> issues — I’ll be in town next week but it’d be great to have some
> preliminary conversations this week so that time can be used
> more efficiently.
>

> discourse if the conversations start straying.
>
> On Nov 30, 2015, at 10:59 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>> If you care about the next release of Stan, you might want
>> to make it to the Stan meeting tomorrow (Tuesday, 1 Dec).
>>
>> The main new features are
>>
>> * variational inference adaptation
>>
>> * container slicing
>>
>> What I don't know is whether
>>
>> * fixes to ADVI satisfy Ben and/or Andrew or
>>
>> * whether the compilers for which slicing through RStan won't compile
>>   matter or not, and if they do, what we need to do to fix it.
>>
>> We could potentially punt and back out the slicing if
>> people think it's important to get out a new version of ADVI
>> for NIPS and people think it's possible to do that in the time
>> we have left (I don't know what the target release date is).
>>
>> We can also punt on the issues we were planning to fix

>> command-line, we have this many issues outstanding:

>>
>> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Numeric integration
messages.body_plain:
Licensing is not a problem at all since it's public domain.

What looks troublesome to me now is how to pass the additional arguments to f:

integrate_function(function f, real lower_limit, real upper_limit, ...)

What would "..." be? A single real? A single eigen vector? Variadic template (!!!)?

On 30/11/2015 21:52, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> All I could find in Boost was the ODE solver, too.  Maybe they don't
> have a simple definite integrator.  The reason I suggested it is licensing
> and minimizing dependencies in Stan.  If you're just doing this for
> a standalone side project, neither of these issues matters.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Nov 30, 2015, at 6:15 PM, Marco Inacio <marcoig...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Why not the one Ben Goodrich suggested? It's C++ and seems pretty simple. Also, I couldn't find boost numerical integrator.
> >
> > On 30/11/2015 21:03, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > I don't think we're going to be supporting Fortran linkage
> > > any time soon --- we have enough build headaches as it is.
> > >
> > > The simplest thing to do would probably to get a boost
> > > integrator, then just autodiff it to start and make sure
> > > you get reasonable results, then do the analytic derivatives.
> > >
> > > Then we can go looking for better integrators, etc. when
> > > the analytic bits are sorted out.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > >
> > > > On Nov 30, 2015, at 4:39 PM, Marco Inacio <marcoig...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > This seems good. I was trying this with the old but good quadpack, but it was hard since I had never worked with importing external Fortran code.
> > > >
> > > > Is your code in a Stan branch?
> > > >
> > > > On 30/11/2015 18:28, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > > > > On Monday, November 30, 2015 at 2:53:37 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > > There are a couple other things like this that Ben

> > > > > I prototyped a little code based on

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, November 30, 2015 at 6:15:08 PM UTC-5, Marco Inacio wrote:
> Why not the one Ben Goodrich suggested? It's C++ and seems pretty
> simple. Also, I couldn't find boost numerical integrator.

Boost doesn't have a general numerical integrator. I think it would be difficult to expose a function like integrate() into the Stan language because no single numerical integration procedure works well on every problem. But Cook's approach works well on functions that decline at a double exponential rate, which covers a lot of things one might want to do in statistics. So, I think something like this could be included in Stan Math and used when appropriate as the back end by functions exposed to the Stan language.

Ben

This made me think that this could be a good test example for MML and VB methods that can integrate over these latent variables.  Worth thinking about as we develop and implement these approximate algorithms.
A

Isn’t this going to be exactly the kind of model with high enough curvature
that MML and VB would yield poor approximations?  I hate to be the wet
blanket, but the same pathologies that make Euclidean HMC slow also
make these approximations slow, so there’s only only a narrow slice in
model space where MML and VB could flourish.

messages.subject: no namespace-level using statements
messages.body_plain:
Please don't include namespace-level includes.

The problem is that then you can't control locally what
gets included, which can lead to name-resolution conflicts,
and it also introduces order dependencies on the files.

See:  http://stackoverflow.com/questions/6175705/scope-of-using-declaration-within-a-namespace

or go straight to Herb Sutter's advice:

  http://www.gotw.ca/gotw/053.htm

That site's awesome, by the way, if you want to study C++ :-)

- Bob

messages.subject: help on Wiener doc
messages.body_plain:
There was a note to update the doc, but I don't understand what's
a comment about what's in Stan and what's a comment about what should
be in Stan.

When it says "prefer it in Stan" is that a suggestion to define a
different density than the one we have?  Or is that what was implemented?

If someone can write up what should get dropped in as a paragraph in
the doc, drop it into this issue

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1617

and I'll get it into the doc.  If that issue's closed, put it in the
next doc issue.

- Bob

P.S.  Here's the note:

>From Joachim Vandekerckhove on stan-users:

Sorry I'm a little late to this party, I had a long summer of travel. The reason we originally implemented the lower-bound hits as negative reaction times was to have a cheap way of encoding what is essentially a bivariate distribution (strictly positive RT and binary response). Because both the RT and the outcome are random variables, the current implementation (with only one bound) isn't entirely satisfactory if at any point we want to generate random numbers from the distribution.

I always liked the negative-RT solution even though it's a little counter-intuitive. I'd probably prefer it in Stan since it's how it works in JAGS... but the more conventional solution would be to make it actually bivariate, and let it operate on a [RT response] pair, where the first is a strictly positive real and the second is a boolean.

messages.body_plain:
On 02/12/2015 00:04, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> There was a note to update the doc, but I don't understand what's
> a comment about what's in Stan and what's a comment about what should
> be in Stan.

I don't think there is anything in his comments meant to be added to the
manual.

> When it says "prefer it in Stan" is that a suggestion to define a
> different density than the one we have?  Or is that what was implemented?

It refers to the author's original version, which is not exactly what is
implemented right now. His original code allowed random variables to be
negative or positive, while the current implementation only allows
positive random variables.

The wiener distribution we have models the amount of time it takes for a
Wiener process to reach an upper bound.

But there's also the possibility of modeling the amount of time it takes
to reach a lower bound. The author's original code modeled this
possibility (of lower bound) using negative random variables.

In the author's R package we do this using a variable resp:

#what you get in Stan
RWiener::dwiener(1.1, 2.1, .3, .55, .4, resp = "upper")

#this would be using -1.1 instead of 1.1 in his original implementation
for Stan
RWiener::dwiener(1.1, 2.1, .3, .55, .4, resp = "lower")

#sum of both densities, only this one integrates to one, wiener is
actually bivariate as he says
RWiener::dwiener(1.1, 2.1, .3, .55, .4, resp = "both")

> Because both the RT and the outcome are random variables, the current implementation (with only one bound) isn't entirely satisfactory if at any point we want to generate random numbers from the distribution.
>

This is interesting, but I'm not sure how well it would behave since
there is discontinuity in the derivatives when we change from lower to
upper (negative random variables to positive random variables).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ADVI status
messages.body_plain:
I have ADVI with adaptation working again in R. Attached are comparisons of posterior means between a couple chains of NUTS, meanfield, and fullrank for 115 non-failing examples in example-models. Many of the failures are unrelated to ADVI but some are things like "stan::variational::advi::adapt_eta: All proposed step-sizes failed. Your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified." when NUTS produces something, which I guess is OK. For the non-failing examples, in R you could do something like

load("matrices.RData")
lapply(matrices, FUN = function(x) round(head(x), digits = 3))

The posterior mean estimates are similar for more examples than before, although fullrank does not seem to be noticeably better than meanfield in the cases where meanfield is considerably different than NUTS. I'll try some from rstanarm later; my guess is that most regression models will be okay with rstanarm's reparameterizations and initial values heuristics.

Ben

It looks like the parameters won't be identifiable on the unconstrained

it be feasible to assign the symmetric unit vector

  1 / sqrt(size(y))

It's the limit of epsilon * (1, ..., 1) as epsilon -> 0.
(Of course, other angles of approach give different limits!).

messages.body_plain:
Unit vectors will never be identifiable until we move past the assumption
that all of our parameters live in R^{n}.  Mathematically this is somewhat
straightforward (there’s a reason I keep all the HMC papers as general
as possible!) but there are all kinds of side effects (means and other
summary statistics are really hard to define on spaces like spheres and
torii).

On Thursday, December 3, 2015 at 2:53:54 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> First, what's the motivation behind reparameterizing unit

In the issue, I put the link to the last time we discussed refactoring this

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/0cXoSwAs3tw/dPT-fAVojdIJ

> It looks like the parameters won't be identifiable on the unconstrained
> scale.  Won't this be bad for adaptation and convergence monitoring
> of the unconstrained parameters?

The unconstrained parameters are identified by the prior assumption that y is i.i.d. standard normal, in which case x = y / sum(y^2) is uniform on the surface of the N-hypersphere and then you could (probably in rare circumstances) make the distribution non-uniform with a sampling statement for x. In Stan < 2.9, using a unit_vector as a parameter would not compile but if it did, the unconstrained hyperspherical angles aren't identified because of the periodicity of the trig functions, but we were basically hoping that they would not wander outside of (-pi,pi) or whatever.

> Second, if zero is a problem for initialization, would
> it be feasible to assign the symmetric unit vector
>
>   1 / sqrt(size(y))
>
> It's the limit of epsilon * (1, ..., 1) as epsilon -> 0.
> (Of course, other angles of approach give different limits!).

messages.subject: protocol buffers, again
messages.body_plain:
I'm following up a little on a previous discussion[1], but I scaled down my ambitions to something that would let me play with Stan and protocol buffers without getting bogged down.

The goal this time around is to build a little I/O around stan::lang::compile so that a protobuf message can go in as input with the Stan program and a message can get returned with the C++ code.  The protobuf version 2 file is attached, probably makes sense to use version 3 but Ubuntu doesn't have the protobuf compiler for that and the differences are minor.

I'm not proposing this as an addition to anything we have right now, but I'd like to go through and put it together in its own repo using boost::asio. Just looking for comments if you're interested.

Krzysztof

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, December 4, 2015 at 5:39:11 AM UTC-5, Allen B. Riddell wrote:
> This is specific task is perhaps more useful than you think. We need
> some standard error format for other cases as well--e.g., when an
> interface submits invalid parameters (e.g., some negative float for a
> parameter that's strictly positive).

I steered clear of this bigger issue for now because there's supposed to be a C++ API refactor that's going to address standardizing input facilities and past discussions have devolved into "protobuf vs. C++ API for Stan".  I'll give it a shot anyway... I think Alan leaves this implicit but here's why the Stan C++ API discussion should also be a protobuf message type discussion:

1) protobuf provides multi-language mappings for strongly-typed language-agnostic data types (see the 'scalar value types' table in [1]).
2) protobuf provides strongly-typed language-agnostic complex types from message definitions.
3) protobuf auto-generates a _message_ API's that a library can be compatible with, but it's an auto-generated API with all the boilerplate that entails.

I think this sets protobuf apart in an API discussion from something that only deals with the format (e.g.-JSON) but at the same time it can't replace a well-formed C++ API.  An important secondary benefit of having the protobuf discussion at the same time as the C++ API discussion would be involving the interface developers in deciding what works well for them without everyone having to have an opinion on the C++ API.

[1] https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3

> Is there any prior art on this? Perhaps someone has already thought hard
> about standardizing a protobuf error message in this kind of situation?

Good point, I was under-thinking this one.  For inter-process (especially remote) communication using the protobuf rpc stuff would make sense[2,3].  The C++ API would be a lot less overhead when used locally but as you've pointed out that's not always easy.

I think it makes sense to stick to just stanc-related protobuf stuff for now and I can do a test-drive of how it would work with some of the grpc server examples once we agree on some preliminary message types.

[2] http://www.grpc.io/docs/
[3] https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/release-0_11/examples/cpp/cpptutorial.md

> discussion on this. Or maybe starting a cmdstan-protobuf repository? (Or

I will start a github repo soon but I wanted to give the broader discussion here a shot first.  I don't think I really got how protobuf could fit into Stan until it went around a few times on the dev list.

> types from message definitions.  3) protobuf auto-generates a
> _message_ API's that a library can be compatible with, but it's an
> auto-generated API with all the boilerplate that entails.
>
> I think this sets protobuf apart in an API discussion from something
> that only deals with the format (e.g.-JSON) but at the same time it
> can't replace a well-formed C++ API.  An important secondary benefit
> of having the protobuf discussion at the same time as the C++ API
> discussion would be involving the interface developers in deciding
> what works well for them without everyone having to have an opinion on
> the C++ API.

Excellent summary. I'd add that protobuf can do zero-copy passing of
data between C++ and R/Python -- which is vital for calculating summary
statistics (including rhat) of large numbers of samples.

> > Is there any prior art on this? Perhaps someone has already thought
> > hard about standardizing a protobuf error message in this kind of
> > situation?
>
> Good point, I was under-thinking this one.  For inter-process
> (especially remote) communication using the protobuf rpc stuff would
> make sense[2,3].  The C++ API would be a lot less overhead when used
> locally but as you've pointed out that's not always easy.
>
> I think it makes sense to stick to just stanc-related protobuf stuff
> for now and I can do a test-drive of how it would work with some of
> the grpc server examples once we agree on some preliminary message
> types.
>
> [2] http://www.grpc.io/docs/ [3]
> https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/release-0_11/examples/cpp/cpptutorial.md
>

Starting with an error message format from gRPC/similar sounds like a good idea.

> >
> > I think opening an issue on Github might be the best place to have a
> > discussion on this. Or maybe starting a cmdstan-protobuf repository?
> > (Or pystan-protobuf or rstan-protobuf, depending on how you imagined
> > prototyping this.)
>
> I will start a github repo soon but I wanted to give the broader
> discussion here a shot first.  I don't think I really got how protobuf
> could fit into Stan until it went around a few times on the dev list.
>

Is there something standing in the way of creating a minimal
protobuf-shim on top of the current C++ API for stanc? This is where I
would start. I'd be willing to try this out with a fork/branch of
PyStan.

Having a working prototype would be a nice first step before we dig into
speccing out all the Messages.

Best,

Allen

it. Until then, some parallel package or shim layer makes sense.

authors:

http://alexey.radul.name/ideas/2013/introduction-to-automatic-differentiation/

with our implementation, including handling what they
call "perturbation confusion", for which I just went with
what seemed like an obvious solution never having seen
the problem mentioned before. I think the author underestimates
the cleverness of the modern C++ compiler.  I'll also write
to him about how we handle custom derivatives "gracefully",
or at least as gracefully as is possible with reverse-mode.

I wrote them a note letting them know about Stan so they can
at least mention it along with other existing systems.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] protocol buffers, again
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, December 4, 2015 at 1:29:38 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> > On Dec 4, 2015, at 8:33 AM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <@gmail.com <http://gmail.com>> wrote:
> >
> > On Friday, December 4, 2015 at 5:39:11 AM UTC-5, Allen B. Riddell wrote:
> >> This is specific task is perhaps more useful than you think. We need
> >> some standard error format for other cases as well--e.g., when an
> >> interface submits invalid parameters (e.g., some negative float for a
> >> parameter that's strictly positive).
> >
> > I steered clear of this bigger issue for now because there's supposed to be a C++ API refactor that's going to address standardizing input facilities and past discussions have devolved into "protobuf vs. C++ API for Stan".
>
> This isn't a vs. thing so much as a layering issue.
> I'm pretty sure we want to maintain a direct C++
> data-structure interface at the API level.

Yes!

>
> Then a protocol buffer would be one way to implement
> an input var_context (not refactored yet) or an
> output_writer (in the middle of being refactored, I think).
>
> >  I'll give it a shot anyway... I think Alan leaves this implicit but here's why the Stan C++ API discussion should also be a protobuf message type discussion:
> >
> > 1) protobuf provides multi-language mappings for strongly-typed language-agnostic data types (see the 'scalar value types' table in [1]).
>
> What's the type system?  Is there an intro to protobuf types
> I can read somewhere?

Yes, look at the table of types in: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3

> > 2) protobuf provides strongly-typed language-agnostic complex types from message definitions.
>
> Could you ealborate on this.  What's a "complex type"?  You
> mean like an array or a dictionary/hashmap/struct?

I was thinking struct.  Look at any simple message definition, say:

message Person {
  required string name = 1;
  required int32 id = 2;
  optional string email = 3;
}

It's composed of types that have well-defined functions for construction/reading/writing in multiple languages but they can serve the same function as a 'struct' in a C program.  They're also allowed to be nested.

>
> > 3) protobuf auto-generates a _message_ API's that a library can be compatible with, but it's an auto-generated API with all the boilerplate that entails.
>
> I don't know what this means.  You're thinking of something
> that might go into a REST-ful server?  Or something that'd
> work through sockets in Docker?

I think this is one of the hard things to get across---protobuf lets you define messages that we can use to talk about how interfaces _could_ communicate (yes, in a way that's inefficient if you can do in-memory instead and really more optimal for client-server interaction).  What they _can't_ do is replace a good C++ Stan API so I think any protobuf thing should rely on stan-dev/stan rather than trying to integrate with it.

messages.body_plain:
Those Google docs are great.  They even have variant
types (oneof).  Thanks.

I don't understand how this is going to work for stanc.
The underlying lang/compiler.hpp has this interface:

input: string for program
       output stream for writing messages

output: string for the C++ class for the program

side effects: write warning messages to the output stream.

The rest of the behavior of stanc in CmdStan or RStan or
PyStan is from the interface.

I like the idea of more structured errors.  Unfortunately,
they're now being written directly to the stream as text
in a way that's plumbed right down to the low-level semantic
actions in lang/grammars/*_def.hpp.

So what's the protocol buffer interface going to look
like in terms of messages?

Is the idea that there'll be a stanc server somewhere
communicating via protocol buffers over sockets (or http or
whatever)?

Or is the idea to rewrite compiler.hpp so that what
gets passed in is a protocol buffer writer instead of
an output stream?   I think an intermediate solution where
we refactor the output produced by the parser and code
generator the same way we're doing the rest of the interface
so that it would take more general callbacks with methods
to do the writing however they want.  One such callback
could be protocol buffers.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] multiple runs of ADVI
messages.body_plain:
For CmdStan, you just fire up four processes from the shell
writing to different files and using different seeds --- the
CmdStan manual has an example.  For the result, we can do R-hat
with the samples for all the runs.

RStan then wraps it all up in R's parallelization for
cross-platform support (at least I think they figured out
how to run it on Windows).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] unit vectors
messages.body_plain:
Thanks --- that jogged my memory.

I'd think the derivative would be 0.

Maybe a better alternative would be to do a slightly
different normalization, like

  x + epsilon / sum(x + epsilon)

where, say epsilon = .01. It's enough to be arithmetically
stable, but not enough to seriously skew initialization.
Probably not a big deal --- I don't find myself initializing
to zero very much any more now that adaptation's better.

- Bob

> On Dec 3, 2015, at 4:15 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Thursday, December 3, 2015 at 2:53:54 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> First, what's the motivation behind reparameterizing unit
> vectors  as
>
>   y / sum(y^2)?
>
> In the issue, I put the link to the last time we discussed refactoring this
>
> https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/0cXoSwAs3tw/dPT-fAVojdIJ
>
> It looks like the parameters won't be identifiable on the unconstrained
> scale.  Won't this be bad for adaptation and convergence monitoring
> of the unconstrained parameters?
>
> The unconstrained parameters are identified by the prior assumption that y is i.i.d. standard normal, in which case x = y / sum(y^2) is uniform on the surface of the N-hypersphere and then you could (probably in rare circumstances) make the distribution non-uniform with a sampling statement for x. In Stan < 2.9, using a unit_vector as a parameter would not compile but if it did, the unconstrained hyperspherical angles aren't identified because of the periodicity of the trig functions, but we were basically hoping that they would not wander outside of (-pi,pi) or whatever.
>
> Second, if zero is a problem for initialization, would
> it be feasible to assign the symmetric unit vector
>
>   1 / sqrt(size(y))
>
> It's the limit of epsilon * (1, ..., 1) as epsilon -> 0.
> (Of course, other angles of approach give different limits!).
>
> What would the "derivatives" be?
>
> Ben
>

combinatorially multimodal like LDA --- nothing's
going to work in that case because the posterior's
intractable.

messages.subject: CmdStan v2.9.0 out now!
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

We've just released the newest version (v2.9.0) of the Stan <https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/releases/tag/v2.9.0> and Stan Math <https://github.com/stan-dev/math/releases/tag/v2.9.0> libraries (v2.9.0)!

Some of the new features in this release:
- General R-like indexing for arrays and vectors!
- Changed unit_vector transformation
- Better adaptation for ADVI
- New core developer member: Krzysztof Sakrejda.

For more details about this particular release, please see the full release notes: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/releases/tag/v2.9.0

The first interface to have the latest features is CmdStan <https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan/releases/tag/v2.9.0>. The release of CmdStan should be compatible with Stan.jl, MatlabStan, and StataStan.

RStan and PyStan will follow shortly.

-- Stan Development Team

P.S. The generalized indexing is really cool. Check out Chapter 5 in the v2.9.0 version of the manual: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/releases/download/v2.9.0/stan-reference-2.9.0.pdf

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] protocol buffers, again
messages.body_plain:
On 12/04, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> Zero-copy passing.  How does that work?  We need to
> get std::vector and Eigen::Matrix instances on the Stan
> side, both of which require copies from raw data
> as far as I know.  Now I can believe you could "zero copy"
> a block of memory, like a pointer.
>

It just works in terms of blocks of memory. Here's an example from the API:

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/cpp/google.protobuf.io.zero_copy_stream

We can just pass around blocks of continuous memory provided their
orientation is right for both Stan/Eigen and R/Python. The point here is
merely that Protocol Buffers will not get in our way if we figure out a
way to do this. This is rather impressive in itself, I think.

> The only reason not to do this now is that it'll all change
> again with the refactor, and I don't think Daniel or Michael
> want more work for that.  So as long as you're happy having it
> on a branch until the Stan 3 refactor lands, there shouldn't
> be a problem.

This seems like a critical point. Can we prioritize finishing up the
refactor insofar as it touches calls to stanc? I think stanc is a fine
place to start finalizing the Stan 3 API in any event and doing so first
would also enable this protobuf experimentation.

Perhaps I jumped the gun. I don't have a problem with the current stanc
API (by which I mean the RStan/PyStan call into lang/compiler.hpp):

In PyStan this is the Cython signature that wraps some C++ code
(duplicated from/in RStan) which calls stan::lang::compile

def stanc(bytes model_stancode, bytes model_name):
    cdef PyStancResult result
    c_stanc(model_stancode, model_name, result)
    return {'status': result.status,
            'msg': result.msg.decode('ascii'),
            'model_cppname': result.model_cppname.decode('ascii'),
            'cppcode': result.cppcode.decode('ascii')}

I can imagine this being replaced by some judicious use of Protocol
Buffers.

Perhaps that's not what Krzysztof had in mind. I imagine it's in the
ballpark.

Best,

Allen

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, December 2, 2015 at 8:35:40 AM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> I have ADVI with adaptation working again in R.

Also, the QR reparameterization seems to expand the scope of linear regression models where ADVI succeeds. For example,

ROOT <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stan-dev/example-models/master/ARM/Ch.4/"
mesquite_data <- read_rdump(paste0(ROOT, "mesquite.data.R"))
mesquite_data$weight <- mesquite_data$weight / 100
mesquite_model <- stan_model(paste0(ROOT, "mesquite.stan"))
ols <- lm(weight ~ diam1 + diam2 + canopy_height + total_height +
            density + group, data = mesquite_data)
MCMC <- sampling(mesquite_model, data = mesquite_data)
MF <- vb(mesquite_model, data = mesquite_data, algorithm = "meanfield")
FR <- vb(mesquite_model, data = mesquite_data, algorithm = "fullrank")

This plain parameterization does not work particularly well (especially for fullrank)

cbind(OLS = coef(ols), MCMC = summary(MCMC)[[1]][1:7,1],
      MF = summary(MF)[[1]][1:7,1], FR = summary(FR)[[1]][1:7,1])

                    OLS      MCMC         MF          FR
(Intercept)   -7.285929 -7.274599 -6.8556038 -1.48931304
diam1          1.896690  1.880635  2.2193935  1.21671570
diam2          3.714621  3.746621  3.3493838  2.28108869
canopy_height  3.556653  3.597312  2.1498317  0.02911905
total_height  -1.017325 -1.061082 -0.6275955 -0.13897944
density        1.312542  1.310747  1.2938405  1.50406152
group         -3.632951 -3.651722 -3.4180468 -1.81033995

But with the QR option in stan_glm()

MF <- stan_glm(weight ~ diam1 + diam2 + canopy_height + total_height +
                density + group, data = mesquite_data, prior = NULL,
               prior_intercept = NULL, prior_ops = prior_options(scaled = FALSE),
              algorithm = "meanfield", QR = TRUE)
FR <- stan_glm(weight ~ diam1 + diam2 + canopy_height + total_height +
                 density + group, data = mesquite_data, prior = NULL,
               prior_intercept = NULL, prior_ops = prior_options(scaled = FALSE),
               algorithm = "fullrank", QR = TRUE)

it does better

cbind(OLS = coef(ols), MCMC = summary(MCMC)[[1]][1:7,1],
      MF = coef(MF), FR = coef(FR))
                    OLS      MCMC        MF         FR
(Intercept)   -7.285929 -7.274599 -7.575135 -6.4010700
diam1          1.896690  1.880635  2.327150  1.2509559
diam2          3.714621  3.746621  3.258451  3.7515768
canopy_height  3.556653  3.597312  3.493274  3.6575743
total_height  -1.017325 -1.061082 -0.770157 -0.9841014
density        1.312542  1.310747  1.209084  1.3232964
group         -3.632951 -3.651722 -3.585129 -3.7281053

Still, it is worrying that ADVI can be so sensitive to things like this.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: an example where glmer is much faster than Stan
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, July 14, 2015 at 11:14:22 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi all.  I came across this example in my applied work.  I’ve scrambled the data and replaced with fake outcomes so as not to violate any privacy with the dataset.  Attached on this message are a zipfile with the data, the Stan code, and the R code.
>
> Here’s the story:  I have a relatively simple hierarchical model (nonnested, with 3 batches of varying intercepts of dimension 51, 15, and 51*15) and 150,000 data points.  Running Stan for 4 chains in parallel, 100 iterations each, takes about 3 times as long as glmer.  But really most people would run Stan for at least 1000 iterations, so Stan is much slower than glmer here.
>
> This is a big motivation for us to get MML working in Stan, also a great example for trying out the new ADVI on a real live problem!
>
> In the attached code I’m fitting the model to a random subset of 20,000 data points, just so it will run faster and you can see what’s going on.
>
> For what it’s worth, glmer and Stan give similar estimates for the regression coefficients but they differ on the estimated variance parameters, where Stan seems to be doing much better.  That’s no surprise because glmer has no regularization on these variance parameters.  Our MML and ADVI will allow these, so they should outperform glmer.
>
> So our goal is to have a quick approx algorithm that runs fast.  The example is a motivator.
>
> P.S.  Stan runs faster on these simulated data than on the real data.  Folk theorem in action, I guess.

stan_glmer with meanfield ADVI ran on the whole fake dataset in about 15 minutes with a QR reparameterization, which is only about twice as long as glmer with its checks turned off. The results look okay

                glmer      stan_glmer

state           0.05464908 0.04413998

messages.subject: numerical integration expose gradient
messages.body_plain:
I tried to use integrate_function in a model and it seems to be working
well, except that it's really slow, making my model unfeasible in practice.

I tracked the bottleneck down to the obvious culprit: the gradient
evaluation... the problem is that we have call var.grad() a really lot
of times to calculate the derivatives.

So the solution I thought of is to allow the user to specify the
derivative of the function to be integrated with respect to each parameter.

So, we would have the simple-to-use version:

        integrate_function(function f, real (data only) lower, real
(data only) upper, vector param)

        Where f has signature
        real function(real x, vector param)

And also the faster version:

        integrate_function_grad(function f, function g, real (data only)
lower, real (data only) upper, vector param)

        Where f has signature the same signature as before and g
(derivative of f) has signature:
        real function(real x, vector param, int n)

        Here n tells the function that you want the derivative of f with
respect to param[n].

After I used integrate_function_grad function, the model ran faster by
at least 2 orders of magnitude I think.

However, if I remember well, the idea of exposing the gradient to users
has already been reject a while ago, so I don't know what you think
about this(?)

The point to do this would be in the Stan 3 refactor
if people think it's worthwhile --- it'll change behavior for

messages.subject: Re: separate PRNG seed for generated quantities
messages.subject_clean: separate PRNG seed for generated quantities
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

The behavior users seem to expect is:

i)  same data, prior and likelihood => same inference
ii) same inference => same prediction

However, the current design leads to different inference if during prediction a random number is used. Given that this is a big effort to implement, I suggest that users are given the following possibility:

1. Do the inference without executing the generated block => i) holds
2. Let users feed the posterior into stan and selectively run only the generated block => ii) holds as well

As far as I recall, Stan 3 is supposed to enable such flexibility, right?

Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I just saw that the cvode branch is MERGED in stan-math & stan!!! Great news! I am looking forward to test this.

I am currently working jointly with the odeSD author to get this stiff integrator into Stan. Would that still be considered? I.e. the integrator promises

- a ~5x speedup over cvode (stiff system)
- is implemented as header only C++
- as Eigen's linear algebra is used which takes advantage of the MKL, those people having it may get another ~2x speedup

The down-side is that odeSD requires second order derivatives and hence hessians must be calculated.

Thoughts on this?

A first (somewhat restricted in functionality) prototype version of this in Stan is doable this month.

Cheers,
Sebastian

PS1: Really, great work! I am glad this happened so fast now.
PS2: Would you consider to let users choose between the non-stiff and stiff cvode integrator? Or is the non-stiff integrator simply the boost integrator?

On Wednesday, December 16, 2015 at 2:00:47 PM UTC-5, Alp Kucukelbir wrote:
> please do share your thoughts and comment!

At the risk of fracturing the discussion into different places on the internet, is parameter tagging the best way to indicate distinctions among ADVI approaches? For example, block diagonal ADVI could be accomplished if there were an option for a user to pass in a proto covariance matrix where elements that were zero are constrained to be zero and elements that were non-zero are free (subject to the positive definiteness restriction). Or ADVI could support a second .stan file that specified how the multivariate normal distribution is parameterized / penalized.

Parameter tagging may be inevitable for MML, in which case having a general framework for it that might also allow ADVI to use it would be nice to have. But given that we haven't ever been close to achieving a consensus on that, I wouldn't want research on ADVI to get stuck waiting for that to happen.

Ben

messages.subject: Fwd: universal prior for reg coefs; first step
messages.subject_clean: universal prior for reg coefs; first step
messages.body_plain:
> ---------- Forwarded message ----------
> From: Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu>
> Date: Wed, Dec 16, 2015 at 2:33 PM
> Subject: universal prior for reg coefs; first step

The first first step was undertaken in 2010 when we twice discussed the implications of this prior for mi (see slides).
For an LKJ distribution on the correlation matrix between X and Y, the distribution of the standardized coefficients is multivariate Pearson type II, which is a special case of an elliptical distribution with a beta generating function
Each marginal standardized coefficient has an unnamed density that can be written in "closed" form with a Gaussian hypergeometric function
The mean exists always, the variance exists if eta > 0.5, the skewness exists if eta > 1, the kurtosis exists if eta > 1.5, etc. Aside from possibly having heavy tails, it does not have a similar shape as a Cauchy density

Many, many steps have been taken since then. I've taught this prior for the last two years in the QMSS class. For a long time, stan_lm in rstanarm was doing this prior. The correlation matrix between X and Y implies a distribution --- that is beta(K/2, eta) --- for the R^2 so prior information about the location (mode, mean, or median) of the R^2 implies a value for eta. There are between one and two problems with this approach:
If you have a distribution of standardized coefficients, you have to unstandardize them to use in the likelihood. For the X variables, it is straightforward to divide the standardized coefficients by their standard deviation but you need to multiply by the marginal standard deviation of Y. I prefer making the marginal standard deviation of Y a primitive that has a Jeffreys prior and you prefer anything but that.
To get the standardized coefficients, you have to pre-multiply a vector by the inverse of a KxK matrix, which is slow in Stan for large K. So, stan_lm() does a QR-based reparameterization that avoids the need to do O(K^3) matrix operations. But now the prior is only over the covariance / correlation between the columns of Q and Y, rather than a whole correlation matrix. This is explained in the vignette: https://github.com/stan-dev/rstanarm/blob/master/vignettes/lm.Rmd

The main obstacles to generalizing these ideas to other distributional forms are:
There are currently no other distributions for a correlation matrix with known properties.
All known alternative ways of constructing a correlation matrix from unconstrained values besides the Stan variant of LKJ require inversion of submatrices. So whatever their properties are, they would need to be worth an O(K^4) transformation from the unconstrained space.
We do have some distributions for covariance matrices that can be rescaled into correlation matrices. I tend to not like the shapes of Wishart or inverse Wishart, but in this context you have the additional problem that there is no information in the data that informs the variances. This makes trouble for HMC but also it is hard to think about what the prior scatter matrix should be.

> To: Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com>, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com>
>
>
> Hi, see attached.  I simulated corr matrices from LKJ distribution, Wishart, and inv-Wishart.  (for the latter two options, we get cov matrices so I rescaled to get corr matrices).  For each, I computed all the regression coefficients (i.e., for a KxK matrix, there are K sets of K-1 coefs, so that’s K*(K-1) coefs).  Just to be clear, I didn’t simulate any data or run any regressions; rather, I simulated corr matrices and from there used the formula to get the regression coefs.
>
> Anyway, for each combination of model (LKJ, WIshart, or inv-Wishart), phi parameter (1, 2, 5, or 10), and dimension (2, 5, 10, 30, or 100), I did 100 simulations and plotted the histogram of the resulting 100*K*(K-1) coefs.  That’s what’s in the attached document.
>
> Interestingly, some of these distributions look Cauchy-like.
>
> See you
> A
>
> P.S.  For LKJ, the “nu” parameter is the same as “phi.”  For Wishart or inv-Wishart, I set nu <- phi + K - 1 to respect the constraint that nu must be at least K-1.
>

What I mean by "outside" is outside of the modeling language.  In
particular, you can have a call to CmdStan like:

I'm not sure what you mean by "slowly mold", but if it means

I also like Bob's idea. It removes the nastiness of putting algorithmic-specific labels into the Stan program, and allows you to change them at runtime. So for MML it would be

./foo mml hyperparameters=“phi" local="alpha"

and ADVI would be

./foo advi meanfield=“w” fullrank=“alpha, sigma”

Similar to external files for specifying inits, the labelling can be read in from an external file. This avoids writing long lists on the command line and not storing them each time. I also feel like we’re converging to this solution (at least in this thread), since the second “.stan” file is essentially trying to do this.

Dustin

See attached figure, where I did LKJ(1), Wishart(K+1) and inv-Wishart(K+1) (in the latter case normalizing so that they gave corr matrices rather than cov matrices) and then I looked at the histogram of all the regression coefs.     K = 5, 1/5/25/50/75/95/99 percentiles are -2.1, -1.1, -0.5,  0.0,  0.5,  1.2,  2.1

  K = 20, 1/5/25/50/75/95/99 percentiles are -2.5, -1.3, -0.5,  0.0,  0.5,  1.3,  2.5
  K = 50, 1/5/25/50/75/95/99 percentiles are -2.5, -1.3, -0.4,  0.0,  0.4,  1.3,  2.5

messages.subject: Re: t_2.5(.5) as a universal prior for scaled linear regression coefficients
messages.subject_clean: t_2.5(.5) as a universal prior for scaled linear regression coefficients
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, December 16, 2015 at 6:43:09 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Strikingly stable, I’d say.  And reasonably fit by a t distribution with 2.5 df and scale .5:
>
> > pfround(quantile(.5*rt(100000, 2.5), c(.01, .05, .25, .5, .75, .95, .99)), 1)
>   1%   5%  25%  50%  75%  95%  99%
> -2.6 -1.3 -0.4  0.0  0.4  1.3  2.6

I agree that it seems to have a limit but
I don't see why we need to match a t distribution to it since we already know its marginal density and could work on deriving its limit as K goes to infinity
The marginal density of a standardized regression coefficient is a bit of a red herring anyway
I don't think setting eta = 1 is an appropriate universal hyperparameter

The critical property of the LKJ-based distribution you are simulating is that

beta' * Cor(X) * beta = R^2 ~ Beta(K/2, eta)

If you just put a bunch of independent t priors on the elements of beta, then you still need a distribution for the correlation matrix of X and even then the quadratic form doesn't equal anything in particular. So, in my opinion, the correct way to interpret this prior is as an informative prior on the unknown R^2 but conditional on the R^2, there is virtually no additional information about the coefficients imparted by the prior.

Thus, I don't think eta = 1 is a great default in light of the Beta(K/2, eta) distribution for the R^2. Clearly, any eta < 1 is usually inappropriate because of the infinite density at 1. Setting eta = 1 puts finite density at 1 but the mode is still 1, which doesn't really make sense for an R^2. For regressions in genetics, I don't think they would presume that the R^2 converges to 1 as K diverges to infinity. Rather, they seem to think that there are a finite number of predictors that actually matter and an infinite number that do not, so the R^2 is bounded away from 1.

The stan_lm() function forces the user to say something about their prior beliefs over the location of the R^2 and derives the value of eta that corresponds to that, which is not universal but I think it is appropriate and reasonably easy for users to deal with.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: t_2.5(.5) as a universal prior for scaled linear regression coefficients
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, December 17, 2015 at 6:45:44 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi, yes, I agree there are some missing steps here.  One idea is that this LKJ thing is that it provides rhetorical support for a certain weak but not completely empty prior.  And it does give us some baseline.  I could try some simulations with other values of eta?

It is a bit misleading to say that the prior is "weak". A Beta(K/2, eta) prior on the R^2 is often quite strong in the sense that you can make it quite concentrated around 0.6 if you thought in advance that the R^2 was 0.6. But all combinations of the prior correlation matrix among the predictors and standardized coefficients that yield a given R^2 are pretty much equally likely under the prior. Using the stochastic representation of the elliptical distribution, we have
beta = sqrt(R^2) * L^{-1} * u
where L * L' is the correlation matrix among the X variables and u is uniformally distributed on the surface of a K-hypersphere. Treating L as an unknown hyperparameter makes this a mixture of elliptical distributions but if you ignore that, you are basically left with the spherical normal R * u and there is no prior information about u except for the restriction that u'u = 1. So, almost all the information in the joint prior is piped through a Beta(K/2, eta) distribution for the R^2.

Ben

messages.subject: Simplify stan::lang::compile by throwing exceptions on errors
messages.subject_clean: Simplify stan::lang::compile by throwing exceptions on errors
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

It would be great for interface writers if errors were standardized. If
we're going to throw exceptions when some "invalid" data is passed to a
function, we should always try to throw exceptions.

One case where something in-between is happening is stan::lang::compile
and I wonder if it couldn't be simplified by just throwing exceptions
when there is a parse error or an error in generating the cpp code.

For example, it seems like we're going to throw errors in the var_context
refactor; here's a bit of Michael's code which throws an exception
when someone passes an invalid `name` to a function:

>   std::vector<size_t> dims = dims_r(name);
>   if (dims.size() != 1) {
>     std::stringstream msg;
>     msg << "Requested the vector " << name
>         << ", but " << name
>         << " is not defined as a vector in variable context"
>         << std::endl;
>     throw std::runtime_error(msg.str());
>   }

Could we simplify ``stan::lang::compile`` by throwing
std::runtime_error`s? Here's the current signature

bool compile(std::ostream* msgs,
             std::istream& stan_lang_in,
             std::ostream& cpp_out,
             const std::string& model_name,
             const std::string& in_file_name = "input") {

Could we do something like this instead, returning ``cpp_out``.

std::string compile(std::string stan_lang_in, const std::string& model_name)

and rely on exceptions to communicate parsing and generator errors?

Packing several parsing errors into an exception doesn't seem so bad to
me -- I think we have lengthy exception error messages elsewhere. If it
is a bad idea then could we standardize what we should do in this kind
of case? Like create a simple struct which encapsulates the possible
results and which could be used in other cases? Here's what compile
could return instead, which would be closer to the existing setup:

struct StanStringResult {
    int error; // 0 or 1
    std::string error_msg;
    std::string result;
} StanResult;

(The current signature for stan::lang::compile also looks a little like
a cmdstand-ism lurking in Stan).

If there's interest in this change, I'm willing to work on it as part of
the overall refactor effort.

Best,

Allen

The gRPC side was pretty straightforward since the original example is text -> text (wrapped in protobuf) and stan::lang::compile also does text -> text. That's a complicated template program for variant types from Boost.
Are you sure it's not just a bug in whatever compiler you're using
or C++11 compatibility (not sure why you're explicitly using C++11).

Which version of the Boost libs are you using?

You'll find a ton of hits for bugs in C++11 and boost::variant
interactions, e.g.,

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/19697405/boostvariant-boostshared-ptrt-wont-compile

https://llvm.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=16965

- Bob

What's happening under the hood is that the stream's
getting plumbed through the parser so that each semantic
action on a rule (for instance, the sampling statement
rule) can write to the stream.

The way to make this more structured isn't to continue
to write to the stream and add a flag, it's to return
a structured set of warnings.

I'm still not clear on why you want to change the behavior
with stanc.  Who's going to catch these exceptions and what
are they going to do with them?  That's always the place to
start with exception design.

Right now, there's two ways to fail.  You can either get
an exception in the code when there's a failed expectation
(such as an opening brace without the expected close brace)
and a parse failure when the program's ill formed for other
reasons.  This is just the behavior inherited from the Spirit
Qi parser, but we could always take a negative return and
throw an exception.

The compile method in stan::lang::compile() is the top level call.
You can see that it gets a boolean return from the underlying
Spirit Qi parser, and it just returns it if it's false.  Otherwise,
it generates the C++, which can't fail and returns true.

If you then look at stan::lang::parse(), which is called by the
compiler, you can see the try/catch blocks where the errors
are trapped and written rather than rethrown.  The reason
for that is that there's nothing higher-level to catch them.

Would you rather that functionality moved up to the calling
program, which could catch an exception?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
What we have now is fine for CmdStan, but I can't speak for
the other interfaces.  I'm sure CmdStan would be easy to
modify for whatever we decide.

The Stan 3 command refactor has the interfaces pass in
callbacks for I/O.  This allows consistent behavior
across interfaces, which is my main goal along with removing
code duplication.

I don't like the idea of having the interfaces catch the
exceptions and deal with them as it will neither reduce
code duplication nor encourage consistent behavior across interfaces.

Right now, we have a callback structure for the interfaces,
but the callback is a simple output stream.  It would be a
lot of work, but straightforward to change the parser API to pass
in a structured callback handler for warnings, errors, etc.

So the question is what should it do?

For example, how much logger-like behavior do you want?
Loggers often configure messages to have log levels, like
fatal error, recoverable error, warning, debug (very verbose mode), etc.
Here's the spec for log4j:

https://logging.apache.org/log4j/1.2/apidocs/org/apache/log4j/Level.html

Then there's the issue of formatting the output --- do you include
thread IDs, time stamps, etc.  And then there's the issue of how a user
or programmatic client configures the logger and where it pipes output.

- Bob

P.S.  I don't like big heterogeneous data structures for returns.
For example, I don't like the return for R's built-in lm() function,
because it's mutable in such a way that allows it to get into
inconsistent states (models mismatching data mismatching estimates).
There are ways to mitigate these problems, but I think the callback
route is much cleaner.  And it allows streaming.

messages.body_plain:
The Stan 3 command refactor has the interfaces pass in callbacks
for I/O.  This allows consistent behavior

across interfaces, which is my goal.

Your suggestion to throw exceptions and have the interfaces
deal with it will allow each interface to go its own way in
config and reporting, which is what we're trying to avoid (though
perhaps in vain).

Right now, we have that callback structure for the interfaces,
but the callback is a simple output stream.  It would be possible
to change that API to have the interfaces pass in a structured

callback handler for warnings, errors, etc.

As far as being happy with what we currently have, it's fine

for CmdStan, but I can't speak for the other interfaces.

I'm sure it'll be easy for CmdStan to adapt to whatever changes
make sense for Python or R.

Refactoring the whole parsing interface to pass in a callback
handler for errors is a lot of work, but I think it would all be
straightforward.  So the thing to do still is figure out what
the callback would be.

I don't think returning a big structure is the right
thing to do.  It's a classic example of a "god object", like
the fit object in RStan, which I also don't like at all.  It's
a despised anti-pattern in the OO community.
See, e.g.,  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_object

So I'd rather stick to callbacks for a presentation layer.
If we do go with something like callbacks, there's the issue of how
much logger-like behavior we want.  Loggers often configure

messages to have log levels, like fatal error, recoverable error,
warning, debug (very verbose mode), etc.
Here's the spec for log4j:

https://logging.apache.org/log4j/1.2/apidocs/org/apache/log4j/Level.html

Then there's the issue of formatting the output --- do you include
thread IDs, time stamps, etc.  And then there's the issue of how a user
or programmatic client configures the logger and where it pipes output.

- Bob

It can be, but it just allocates a new variable on the stack each time.
Passing in the accumulator would be most efficient.  So on the inside,
you get

  sum(0 + j[1], 0 + j[2], ..., 0 + j[n])

whereas doing it on the outside you get

  0 + j[1] + j[2] + ... + j[n]

and with an accumulator you get the ideal

  sum(j[1], j[2], ..., j[n])

and if you pass in the global accumulator, it's a bit better still
because those j[1]...j[n] just go in the global accumulator's sum.

because it'll be most efficient and given that it's not some complex
template metaprogram, won't adversely affect compile time (no recursion,
just simple matching).

meta-defined "concepts" (meta in the sense that they aren't

programming.  I agree that it's easier to understand as

than a templated concept.  The tension is because the templated
approach is faster.  The in-between "solution" is the CRTP, like
Eigen uses for its matrix classes, though we've also seen what
a pain that is in practice.

>  B b = B();

>

> templated printer 1
>
>

> C++ allows linking in new instances, so it can't decide statically

Bob, could you take a look into the repository at github.com/sakrejda/protostan <http://github.com/sakrejda/protostan>?  I don't have the permissions to add
a new repo to stan-dev but I did set up a new repo that depends on
stan-dev/stan and stan-dev/math as submodules.  There's a little README.md,
a wrapper around stan::lang::compile, a tests for the wrapper that matches the
test for stan::lang::compile, and a compile-run.sh that should be a complete recipe for compiling and running the (two) tests.

My questions about this are:

1) Does this make sense as a stan-dev repo? If so, could you make a stan-dev fork?
2) What should the namespace setup be like?  At the moment it's stan::proto::function_name and I was expecting it to just be flat (so that that's where someone writing an interface would fine all the external API functionality)  I'm open to doing something different, I have no experience with this.
3) Does the directory structure make sense?  Again, I have little experience with making something other developers would find intuitive so I just monkeyed what Stan has (with the potential complication of code in multiple languages, not just C++).
4) I'm thinking of this as a sketch so if there's something I can do to flesh out the intent of the project I'm open to input.
5) I'm working on a writer_callback that would make sense in this context but I can't quite tell which parts of Stan are meant to be an "external" API (the stuff in "services" maybe?) So suggestions on which parts to wrap are also welcome.

Thanks for any pointers!

Krzysztof

There is a lot of complexity added with the protobuf dependencies
and the protobuf code generation so unless there's a compelling
reason I think it makes sense to keep it a separate repo.  If
we find a compelling reason to merge things in the future that's
fine too.

> What are the licenses for the dependencies for protocol buffers?

> I'm afraid I don't understand what I'm looking at, for

> State?  Is that some kind of return code enum?  And cpp code is
> what's produced?  What's the 2, 3, and 4 for?  I could guess a
> default value for state, but cpp_code and messages are numbers.

What's a proto file: the .proto file plays the same kind of role as
a .stan file in that it can be translated by the protobuf compiler
("protoc") into C++ (or other languages).

What's up with the numbers: protobuf makes you number your fields
and that has some implications for efficiency and backwards/forwards
compatibility and efficiency.

- Efficiency: items in a messages with field numbers under... 16
(or some small number like that, don't remember now) take less
storage space.  I think this only really matters when you transmit
a LOT of really small messages.

- Compatibility: the generated code can be used to check whether a
field exists, so if you deprecate and remove a field but keep the fields
numbered (leaving a useless hole in the numbering) the code previously
generated from the .proto file can continue working (assuming it doesn't
require the presence of the deprecated field).  If you do renumber
fields you break all the auto-generated code.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] protocol buffers, again
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, December 28, 2015 at 4:29:20 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> But what I'm trying to understand is who you are expecting
> to use this interface and for what.  It's hard to even read
> it without understanding what it's for.

Ok, let's pretend we needed an interface for R.  The interface author
could deal with R -> C -> C++ and associated memory management.

As an alternative the interface author could write their interface code
around constructing protobuf messages following this guide:

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RProtoBuf/vignettes/RProtoBuf-quickref.pdf

Then the step of calling Stan would involve only calling simple functions , passing protobuf messages as argument, and receiving protobuf messages in return.  The vignette linked above show that, for the example message "message", to code for constructing it is as simple as:

message <- new( tutorial.Person, id = 0,
 name = "Romain Francois",
 email = "fran...@huh.org" )
message[[ "name" ]] <- "Romain"

Now if we pretend we wanted a website driven Stan interface written by someone who knows PHP, they could do the same kind of song and dance in PHP.  Following
https://github.com/allegro/php-protobuf/#example here's an example of using PHP to construct a protobuf message (the .proto file is at the link):

<?php
    require_once 'pb_proto_foo.php';

    $foo = new Foo();
    $foo->setBar(1);
    $foo->setBaz('two');
    $foo->appendSpam(3.0);
    $foo->appendSpam(4.0);

    $packed = $foo->serializeToString();

    $foo->clear();

    try {
        $foo->parseFromString($packed);
    } catch (Exception $ex) {
        die('Upss.. there is a bug in this example');
    }

    $foo->dump();
?>

Anyway, this really limits the complexity of the actual external calls from any given language and should make it easy to write a first interface. Given the promises protobuf makes about efficiency and limiting copying I don't think it would be a bad first interface.  I don't know if that vision will work out in the end but if Stan is successful enough to have interfaces to a dozen more languages I think this approach would limit the maintenance headaches.  I recognize that these goals overlap with the Stan 3 goals but I don't know enough about Stan 3 goals to know how much overlap there is.

> By dependencies, I meant are there any libraries you need
> to include and what are their licenses?  Stan has dependencies
> currently on Boost and Eigen, but nothing else.  Is this going
> to add new library dependencies?  For example, who wrote the protobuf
> compiler?

If you rolled it into stan itself there would be one dependency for the supporting protobuf library.  The protobuf compiler license is pretty simple:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/LICENSE

The key bit is:

"Code generated by the Protocol Buffer compiler is owned by the owner of the input file used when generating it.  This code is not
standalone and requires a support library to be linked with it.  This
support library is itself covered by the above license."

Sorry this is confusing, I only brought it back up here you
sounded interested in seeing the code.  It'll only make more
sense once we figure out exactly what we want to wrap and
produce a functional example.

Krzysztof

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] protocol buffers, again
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

The protocol buffer interface to the Stan C++ API is a C API. Having a C
API for Stan makes writing an interface far easier.

There are two major applications I can imagine -- here I'll just echo
what Krzysztof said:

- Python, Julia, Go, R, etc. could interface with the C API without
  needing to write any C or C++ code at all. In most of these languages
  it's very simple to wrap C code but considerably harder to interface
  with C++ code.
- ServerStan -- some sort of streaming, multiplexed HTTP2-based RPC
  version of Stan in the cloud (using Google's gRPC, I would think).
  Could be extremely cool. People could just install a thin client on
  their computer. Having such a thing would make a browser-based Stan
  very easy to do (the hard part would be the UI).

Best,

Allen

There are a couple of options here. Protocol buffers are a serialization
format with support in most languages. I'm intrigued by the option of
writing a shim (in C++ with a bunch of extern "C" functions accepting
and returning Protocol Buffer-formatted buffers) which could be used
directly by a foreign function library. Doing so could lighten PyStan
considerably. This approach is a bit different than the ServerStan idea
(which would communicate by passing protocol buffer messages over a
network socket).

>
> So I don't understand where C comes in.  You seem to suggest
> below that the interface writer (e.g., someone writing
> a replacement for PyStan) will just use the interface
> language (say Python).
>
> That would mean everything from exceptions to
> streaming output will be done with protocol buffers.
>
> > Having a C
> > API for Stan makes writing an interface far easier.
>
> Is that true for R, too?
>

Maybe. In theory you might be able to use the built-in foreign function
interface instead of Rcpp.

I'm not exactly sure what will be easiest. It might be easier to run an
instance of ServerStan locally and have a thin client talk to that. In
that case PyStan could become a bundled distribution of a thin
client+ServerStan.

> > There are two major applications I can imagine -- here I'll just echo
> > what Krzysztof said:
> >
> > - Python, Julia, Go, R, etc. could interface with the C API without
> >  needing to write any C or C++ code at all. In most of these languages
> >  it's very simple to wrap C code but considerably harder to interface
> >  with C++ code.
>
> You mean that Python would write Python code to call a protocol buffer
> that hides all the C++ details?  I just don't see where C comes into the picture.
>
> > - ServerStan -- some sort of streaming, multiplexed HTTP2-based RPC
> >  version of Stan in the cloud (using Google's gRPC, I would think).
> >  Could be extremely cool. People could just install a thin client on
> >  their computer. Having such a thing would make a browser-based Stan
> >  very easy to do (the hard part would be the UI).
>
> And affording the cycles!  So you'd use Google's gRPC to connect
> to a dockerized version of Stan?  All these interfaces make my head
> spin.

Ok, so a public version of ServerStan would certainly have to include
some IP-address based rate limiting.

messages.subject: new density notation
messages.body_plain:
I want to run this by everyone on stan-dev before
creating the issue and starting to work on it.

1.  New density expression with normalization and vertical bar:

  cauchy<norm=true>(y | mu, sigma)

defaults to norm=false:

  cauchy(y | mu, sigma)

2. New increment log density statement:

  ld << cauchy(tau | 0, 2.5),
        normal(beta | 0, 2),
        bernoulli_logit(y | x * (tau * beta));

comma-separated values all added to log density accumulator.

3.a.  Deprecate the use of any function ending in "_log" and
go with the above form.

b.  Maintain support for user-defined functions ending in "_log"
to be used this way and keep our density library in C++ ending in "_log".

c.   Make a local variable available to functions such as norm__
with the value of the <norm=...> specification (0 or 1 as int).

4.  Deprecate use of the sampling statement:

   y ~ foo(theta);

5.  Rewrite all the examples in the manual!

NOTE ON BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY:  The proposal is to maintain backward
compatibility but raise deprecation warnings.  Alternatively, we could
just capture old syntax and print specialized update warnings.

- Bob

lp << density1 << density2;

makes more sense to me.

In any case, I suggest to try out this new scheme on people who are more statisticians than programmers, i.e. I think someone having a programming background will absorb this easily, but I am not so sure about those people without a programming background.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] new density notation
messages.body_plain:
I was thinking about just that.

* introduce "=" as a synonym for "<-" in assignment statements
  and deprecate "<-"

* use "+=" for increment statements

* introduce operators "++" and "--" for expressions
  - definitely prefix
  - optionally postfix

Stan already includes a deprecated variable "lp__" which holds
the log density accumulator.  We don't want people to assign
to that variable --- too easy to lose terms, including the Jacobian.
So we just want an increment.  And we want to access its value,
and I thought we'd added a function, but I don't see it;  so we need

* function log_density() that returns current value of accumulator

And then we can get rid of lp__ altogether in Stan 3.

There's the remaining question of whether we

* reserve ld as a variable or function name

It won't conflict in the streaming increment notation.
The "<<" is C++ streaming notation and we're thinking of it as streaming
additive terms to the log density accumulator.

- Bob
